Welcome to the PULSE developer documentation. Connect your product catalogue and storefront to
PULSE, find out which missing product information is costing you sales, and prove each fix worked.
Follow the steps below to get your account ready, or jump straight into the
quickstart (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/quickstart).

For PULSE merchants. 
These docs are for online merchants with a PULSE merchant account and an active
subscription, and for the developers they bring in to connect it. Every request needs an API
key, and a key comes from your account's dashboard. If your company does not have an account
yet, see the plans and create one.

PULSE is a service for e-commerce merchants. It reads your product catalogue and measures whether
it can answer the questions shoppers ask before they buy: which screen size, will it fit, does it
work with what they already own. Where it cannot, PULSE tells you which missing piece of
information costs the most buying decisions, which repair to make first, and afterwards whether
the repair worked.

It is sold as products you can buy on their own, each one an API:

- Decision Audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-audit). Send one category of products; get back the attributes worth recording,
ranked by how many shoppers need them.
- Decision Verification (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-verification). Send the repaired catalogue; get back what changed, attribute by
attribute.
- Return Verification (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/return-verification). Send your orders with the reasons
people gave; see which missing facts go with returns, and whether a repair moved them.
- Decision Monitor (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-monitor). Send each new export; see which shelf slipped
since the last one.
- Promotion Audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/promotion-audit). Send your promotion history; see which offers
paid for themselves after returns and failed deliveries, and where to give nothing.
- Storefront products (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/storefront), optional: the Decision API, Search, Recommendations and
category pages rank your catalogue for each visitor from what their session implies, with the
reason behind every score.

PULSE is made by Resolve Labs. The marketing site, which covers why rather than how, is
thepulseapi.com.

chunks.h: The advantage of starting at the catalogue
chunks.t:
Most tools in this space rank what a shopper sees. PULSE asks the question underneath that one:
can your catalogue answer what they came to find out at all?

A shopper leaves without buying for one of two reasons. Either they could not find the product,
or your catalogue could not tell two products apart. The second is larger and almost nobody
measures it. On a 216-product test shelf we built, 156 generated laptop listings and 60 real marketplace listings, 94 products remain indistinguishable 
after every question a shopper could answer, because the attributes that would separate them are
not recorded anywhere. No ranking model fixes that. Only recording the attribute does.

So your own product data is the foundation, and everything here is a route to working with it:

chunks.h: The advantage of starting at the catalogue
chunks.t:
- Measuring a catalogue with the audit endpoint (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/audit). It takes a category export
and returns the attributes worth recording, ranked by how many shoppers need them rather than
by how empty the column is. Stateless, and it stores nothing unless you ask it to.
- Proving a repair worked with the verify endpoint (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/audit), which runs the same
measurement on the repaired export and reports what moved, attribute by attribute. It reads
your catalogue rather than your traffic, so there is nothing to wait for.
- Reading live sessions with the browser SDK (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/sdk), which sends signals and gets back a
ranking of your catalogue against what the session implies, every score with a per-factor
breakdown. This is the only part that touches your storefront, and it is optional.
- Integrating where you already work, through framework guides (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/frameworks),
storefront platforms (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/platforms) and server libraries (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/backend) for eight languages.
- Letting an agent read these docs through the MCP server (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/mcp), so an assistant answers
from the documentation itself rather than from memory.

chunks.h: The advantage of starting at the catalogue
chunks.t:
Nothing goes on your site to begin with. The first useful answer comes from a file.

chunks.h: Why four of them are free
chunks.t:
/event, /exposure and /outcomes are how you prove the ranking worked. Charging for measurement makes
switching it off the rational move, which blinds the learning loop and destroys the value case
in the same stroke.

/suggest fires on every keystroke. Metering it like /search would bill per character typed,
so someone spelling out a query would pay ten times for one search.

Usage is grouped by the first path segment. 
/track and /track/behavior are both billed as track, and /catalog/ranked,
/catalog/audit and /catalog/verify are all billed as catalog. Your invoice shows a line
per operation rather than one total, because /search costs real compute and /session
costs almost nothing.

There is a second, much larger API behind a JWT, not an API key: organizations, users,
roles, API keys, catalogue management, billing and subscriptions. That is the management plane

Treat anything undocumented as unsupported. 
Routes exist that are not on this page. Some are internal, some are reachable only with a
login, and some resolve at the gateway and are not served downstream. If it is not written
down here, do not build on it.

Sign in to the dashboard (https://app.thepulseapi.com), open Integration → API keys, and

--- --- 
Format Always pk_live_ followed by base64url randomness 
Publishable Designed to be visible in browser code. It can send signals and read rankings, nothing else 
Scoped Belongs to one organization and cannot read another's data 
Shown once The full value is returned only at creation. Only the hash is stored 
Revocable Revocation is immediate

POST /catalog/audit and /catalog/verify, which grade catalogue data rather than rank it.

The ranking endpoints answer "which products first". These two answer a different question:
can this catalogue answer the questions shoppers are asking of it at all. 

Both take a CSV as a string in the body rather than a file upload. An audit is a pure function
over text, so multipart would add a parser, a temporary file and a cleanup path for no gain at a
size where a category export is tens of kilobytes.

Neither call stores anything unless you ask it to.

Why the horizon is not guessed for you. 
Without it the response carries no action. Comparing "ask the shopper" against "record the
fact once" needs to know how many shoppers the fact would serve, and picking a number on your
behalf would bury the assumption the whole comparison rests on.

chunks.t:
POST /decide tells an AI agent which candidate products meet a shopper's requirements, which fail, and which the listing cannot tell, with the missing facts named.

An agent asked to recommend a product either trusts what it thinks it read or refuses.
POST /decide gives it a third answer: exactly what each listing shows. Per candidate and per
requirement it says meets, fails or unknown, and gives each product a verdict of
fits, fails or cannot_tell, with the facts that are missing.

It is what the MCP tool resolve_products calls. See MCP for agents (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/mcp).

Each product also carries requirements, one entry per requirement with its status, the
value decided on and its source. The response repeats what the query was understood to mean
as intent: the product words, the budget, who it is for.

Field Required Meaning 
--- --- --- 
query no The shopper's words. A budget in it ("under 2 triệu", "below RM2,000") becomes a price requirement 
requirements no Up to 20, each { attribute, op, value }. op is lte, gte, eq or neq 
products yes 1 to 50 candidates, each { id, title?, description?, price?, attributes? } 

Send at least one requirement, or a query that states a budget. With nothing to check, the call
answers 400 rather than calling every product a fit.

- Fields first. A value in attributes or price is the merchant's word and wins.
- Then the text. A fact found only in the title or the description still counts, marked
"source": "extracted". Today the text reader knows laptop facts: ram and storage in GB,
screen in inches, and cpu.
- Never a guess. A value that is missing, or stated in a way that cannot be compared, is
unknown, and the product is cannot_tell. A gap in the listing never counts as a pass.

Each call counts as one decision on your plan. It reads nothing about a visitor and stores
nothing, so it needs no session.

The real response shape, and what each code means.

Every error has the same envelope.

correlationId is the useful field. 
Quote it when you report a problem. It is how a single request is found in the logs, and it
turns "ranking looked wrong yesterday" into one lookup.

Code HTTP What it usually means 
--- --- --- 
BAD_REQUEST 400 Malformed body, or an empty body with a JSON content type 
UNAUTHORIZED 401 Missing, wrong, or revoked key. Check the header is x-api-key 
FORBIDDEN 403 The key is valid but not for this organization's data 
NOT_FOUND 404 No such route. Check the /api/v1 prefix 
TOO_MANY_REQUESTS 429 Rate limited at the gateway 
SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE 503 A downstream service is failing fast behind its circuit breaker

chunks.h: Two that are worth knowing apart
chunks.t:
401 on every request, including ones that worked yesterday. 
A revoked or expired key returns 401 exactly like a typo. Keys can be given an expiry at
creation. Check the dashboard before debugging your code.

404 on a path that exists in the docs. 
The base URL includes the version: https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1. A request to
thepulseapi.com/v1/... reaches the marketing site, not the API, and will not look like an
API error at all.

POST /exposure, which is what makes ranking quality measurable.

Ranking cannot be graded without knowing what was actually shown. A click rate over results
nobody saw is not a measurement.

exposure buffers, because a product grid renders many items at once and one request per card
would be absurd. flushExposures sends what is pending, and the SDK also flushes on page hide.

Send what rendered, not what you requested. 
If you asked for 24 and showed 12 above the fold, the honest exposure is what the shopper could
actually see. Over-reporting exposure makes your own ranking look worse than it is.

c.s:
pulse.exposure(decisionId, items);   // buffered
await pulse.flushExposures();        // send now

chunks.t:
POST /interventions/audit, /decide and /landed. Judge offers on orders kept after returns and failed deliveries, choose per group including giving nothing, and compare landed prices.

Three stateless calls behind the Promotion Audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/promotion-audit). Nothing is stored,
and nothing is estimated for you: every rate is yours.

Each offer has a kind: none, price, voucher, shipping, repair or bundle. Every
group needs exactly one none, the comparison everything is judged against.

Your history, one row per group and offer, including the periods with no offer.

An abridged response. erc is expected retained contribution per shopper; miv is its gain over
doing nothing.

Return reasons are read like Return Verification (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/return-verification): "too small" is a
fact the listing could have given; "damaged in transit" and "wrong item" are not.

reason is one of:

Value Means 
--- --- 
beats_doing_nothing choice wins, even with its purchase rate at the cautious end of its interval 
nothing_beats_doing_nothing No offer you measured did better than none 
not_clear_of_noise An offer wins only at the point estimate; test names it 
untested_option_could_win An offer with too little history might win; test names it 
baseline_not_measured The no-offer row itself is too thin to compare against 

An arm needs at least 1,000 visitors and 30 orders to count as measured.

chunks.t:
POST /outcomes, which tells PULSE what happened to each order line, so ranking can favour the purchases that stay bought.

A purchase is not the end of the story. Some orders come back, and some never arrive. Reporting
what happened to each order line lets the retention factor rank on purchases that are kept,
not only on purchases that are made. See what a score is made of (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/ranking#what-a-score-is-made-of).

Send it from your server, whenever an order line changes state: placed, delivered, returned,
refunded, cancelled. Reporting the same line again updates it rather than adding a second one, so
send the whole line each time it moves.

Returns 202 with { "written": 1 }. Up to 1,000 lines per request.

- organizationId must be the organisation your API key belongs to; any other is refused with
403.
- The same line twice in one request keeps the last one.
- A line already reported as returned stays returned if a later report says kept.

c.s:
curl -X POST "https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/outcomes" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: pk_live_..." \
  -d '{
    "organizationId": "org_abc123",
    "lines": [
      {
        "orderId": "SO-10442",
        "merchantProductId": "sku-123",
        "decisionId": "3f1c0b2e-...",
        "orderedAt": "2026-10-01T09:30:00Z",
        "status": "returned",
        "paymentMethod": "cod",
        "returnReason": "I want to return item in original / sealed condition",
        "reassessedReason": "Size different from expected",
        "returnedAt": "2026-10-12T15:00:00Z",
        "returnQuantity": 1,
        "refundMinor": 49000000,
        "currency": "VND"
      }
    ]
  }'

chunks.t:
Field Required Meaning 
--- --- --- 
orderId yes Your order id. Together with merchantProductId it identifies the line 
merchantProductId yes The product's id in your catalogue, as synced to PULSE 
orderedAt yes When the order was placed, ISO 8601 
status yes kept, returned, refunded, partial, cancelled or failed_delivery 
decisionId no The decisionId of the ranking the shopper bought from. Joins the outcome to that ranking 
paymentMethod no For example cod or card 
returnReason no The reason the buyer chose 
reassessedReason no The marketplace's own reading after reviewing the case, such as Shopee's Reassessed Return Reason. Used in place of the buyer's when present 
returnedAt for a return When it came back. Required when status is returned, refunded or partial 
quantity, returnQuantity no Units ordered on the line (default 1), and units that came back. Returns count units, so one of five returned is 20%, not 100% 
refundMinor, currency no The refund in minor units (cents, dong), and its currency 

No personal data. 
There is no field for a name, phone number, address or email, and any field not listed above is
dropped before it is stored. Nothing about the buyer is needed.

Only returns that better product information could have prevented affect ranking: wrong size,
not as described, not compatible, wrong colour or material. Transit damage, counterfeits, a wrong
item sent, empty parcels and refused cash-on-delivery orders are stored but never count against a
product, because no listing change fixes them. Cancelled and failed deliveries are not orders the
product could have kept, so they are left out of its delivered orders too.

chunks.h: Link the purchase to the ranking

chunks.h: What a score is made of
chunks.t:
Every ranked product carries the factors that produced its score. Each is a number from 0 to 1, and
the score is their weighted average over the factors that had something to go on. A factor with
no data behind it is left out of the average, not counted as zero, so a catalogue that sends no
ratings is not marked down for it.

Field What it measures Needs 
--- --- --- 
personaBoost How well the product fits what this session is shopping for a few signals in the session 
qualityBoost Rating, how many reviews stand behind it, sales, discount ratingAverage, reviewCount, quantitySold, compareAtPrice 
baseScore How well the product matches the query's words a query 
priceBoost Whether the price sits where this session's budget does price 
affinityBoost Attribute preferences recorded for this category category affinities 
audienceFit Whether the product's shelf is aimed at who is probably looking audience data for the category 
retention How often the product comes back for a reason the listing could have prevented, against the rest of the shelf. 0.5 is the shelf's own rate deliveredOrders, evidenceReturns

chunks.h: Queries in the shopper's own words
chunks.t:
baseScore is computed on the words that name a product. Before scoring, PULSE reads the rest of
the query for what it says about the purchase: a price limit, who it is for, the occasion, and

English, with or without Vietnamese accents.

Query Read as

S$150, RM2,000, ₱2,500, 3,000 บาท, 750rb and 2 juta. They are compared with your price

retention is off until PULSE has return history. Without it, ranking is exactly what it would
otherwise be. There are two ways to give it: report order outcomes (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/outcomes) and PULSE
keeps the counts itself, or send the totals on each product as below.

- deliveredOrders counts delivered orders only. Leave out cancelled, unpaid and failed ones.
- evidenceReturns counts returns for a reason better product information could have prevented:
wrong size, not as described, not compatible. Never transit damage, counterfeits, a wrong item
sent, or a refused cash-on-delivery order, because no listing change fixes those.
- A product with few orders is pulled toward the shelf's rate rather than taken at face value, and a
product you send no history for scores 0.5.

Add margin (what a kept order contributes) and returnCost (what one return costs you), in one

sessions is ranked without retention at all, so a product ranked down still gets the chance to

chunks.h: The API is versioned. The guides are not.
chunks.t:
Versioned Why 
--- --- --- 
API reference Yes, /api/v1 It is a contract. A request you wrote last year has to keep working, so the page describing it has to keep existing 
Guides, concepts, frameworks No They describe behaviour, not a contract. "How inference works" has no v1 and v2 
SDK reference No The SDK follows the API. Where a method needs a minimum version, the page says so inline 

The version in the docs URL matches the version in the request URL:

Only v1 exists. 
There has never been another. The path carries the version anyway, because a URL is cheap to
choose now and expensive to change once people have linked to it.

c.s: https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/track   →   /api/v1/track

chunks.h: What counts as a breaking change
chunks.t:
A new major version happens only when an existing, correct request would start behaving
differently.

Breaking: needs a new version. 
- Removing an endpoint, a field, or an accepted value
- Renaming anything in a request or response
- Making an optional request field required
- Narrowing a type, for example a string that becomes an enum
- Changing the meaning of a field while keeping its name. This is the worst one, because nothing fails loudly

Not breaking: ships into the current version. 
- Adding a new endpoint
- Adding an optional request field
- Adding a field to a response. Parse responses permissively: unknown fields will appear
- Adding a new value to an output enum, unless the docs say the set is closed
- Making a validation message clearer

chunks.h: What we owe you when a version changes
chunks.t:
1. A new path, /api/v1/v2, with v1 still published and still working 
2. A migration page naming every behavioural difference, not a summary
3. A deprecation notice on each v1 page pointing at its v2 equivalent
4. A stated end date for v1, not "eventually"

@thepulseapi/sdk (https://www.npmjs.com/package/@thepulseapi/sdk) follows
semver (https://semver.org) and tracks the API rather than mirroring it.

While the SDK is 0.x. 
Pre-1.0, a minor version may contain a breaking change. That is what 0.x means in semver,
and it is worth pinning an exact version until 1.0.

The CDN build is versioned the same way, with an immutable path per release and a floating major:

PULSE from a server, in any language that can send JSON over HTTPS.

There is no PULSE library for your backend language, and you do not need one. Every endpoint is
POST, every body is JSON, and authentication is one header.

That is the whole integration surface. The guides in this section are the same three calls
written idiomatically per language, so you can copy one and delete the rest.

Content-Type: application/json
x-api-key: pk_live_...

chunks.h: Which calls belong on a server
One thing to get right first
chunks.t:
sessionId and organizationId are required on nearly every call, and both come from the body
rather than from the API key. A request without them returns 400 with the field named. See
Send signals (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/track).

A session is yours to name. It is a string you generate, up to 128 characters, and the only rule
is that the same shopper keeps the same one. If the browser is already running the SDK, read it
with pulse.getSessionId() and pass it to your server rather than inventing a second session for
the same person.

There is one kind of key. 
Keys are pk_live_, publishable, and the same key works from a browser and from a server.
There is no separate secret key today, which means a key leaked from your server is no worse
and no better than one read out of your page source. Scope and rotate accordingly.

A typed HttpClient, registered once, injected where it is needed.

No package to install. HttpClient and System.Text.Json are in the framework.

AddHttpClient is what you want rather than new HttpClient(): it pools handlers and rotates
them, which is the difference between reusing connections and exhausting sockets under load.

Property names. 
System.Text.Json serialises anonymous object members verbatim, so sessionId stays
sessionId. If you swap in a named class with PascalCase properties, set
JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase or the API will reject the body as missing its required fields.

net/http and encoding/json. Nothing to install.

Pass the request context. 
Threading r.Context() through means a shopper who navigates away cancels the ranking call
instead of leaving it running against a response nobody will read.

java.net.http, in the JDK since 11. No dependencies beyond a JSON library.

HttpClient is thread safe and pools connections, so build one and keep it. In Spring, that
means a @Bean, not a new inside a controller.

Two timeouts, not one. 
connectTimeout on the client and timeout on the request do different jobs. Set only the
first and a server that accepts your connection and then stalls will hold the thread
indefinitely.

The SDK runs on the server too, and fetch is there if you would rather not install it.

@thepulseapi/sdk is isomorphic. The same package works in Node, so a server-rendered page can
use the client it already knows.

Turn autoTrack off on a server. 
It exists to capture device, referrer and time from the browser. On a server those describe
your datacentre, and sending them pollutes the session with signals about a machine nobody
shopped from.
Node 18 and later ship fetch, so the whole integration is one function.

cURL from the standard library, and Guzzle where a framework already ships it.

For the browser half of a PHP app, see the Laravel guide (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/frameworks/laravel). This page is the
server half: calls your PHP makes itself.

Guzzle is already there, wrapped as Http.

Keep it out of the view. 
A ranking call inside a Blade template runs on every render with no timeout you control and no
way to fall back. Resolve it in the controller, pass the result in, and render catalogue order
when it fails.

<?php

namespace App\Services;

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Http;

class Pulse
{
    public function rankedCatalog(string $sessionId, int $limit = 24): array
    {
        return Http::withHeaders(['x-api-key' => config('services.pulse.key')])
            ->timeout(5)
            ->post('https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/catalog/ranked', [
                'sessionId' => $sessionId,
                'organizationId' => config('services.pulse.org'),
                'limit' => $limit,
            ])
            ->throw()
            ->json();
    }
}

requests or httpx, plus where the call belongs in Django and FastAPI.

Or requests, if it is already in the project. Both work; httpx is here because it gives you
the async client FastAPI wants without a second dependency.

Build the client once at module level, not per request. httpx.Client keeps a connection pool
and creating one per view throws that away.

Use the async client, and hold it on the app so it is created once and closed on shutdown.

Give it a timeout. 
Neither requests nor httpx has a default timeout in the shape most people expect. A
ranking call that hangs will hold a worker until something else gives up. Five seconds is
generous; the call is usually tens of milliseconds.

import os
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI

BASE = "https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1"
ORG = os.environ["PULSE_ORG_ID"]


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.pulse = httpx.AsyncClient(
        base_url=BASE,
        timeout=5.0,
        headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["PULSE_API_KEY"]},
    )
    yield
    await app.state.pulse.aclose()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


@app.get("/ranked/{session_id}")
async def ranked(session_id: str, limit: int = 24):
    response = await app.state.pulse.post(
        "/catalog/ranked",
        json={"sessionId": session_id, "organizationId": ORG, "limit": limit},
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

require "json"
require "net/http"
require "uri"

class Pulse
  BASE = URI("https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1").freeze

  def initialize(api_key:, organization_id:)
    @api_key = api_key
    @organization_id = organization_id
  end

  def track(session_id, signals)
    post("/track", sessionId: session_id, signals: signals)
  end

  def ranked_catalog(session_id, limit: 24)
    post("/catalog/ranked", sessionId: session_id, limit: limit)
  end

  def session(session_id)
    post("/session", sessionId: session_id)
  end

  private

  def post(path, **body)
    # organizationId is required on nearly every endpoint and is read from the body,
    # not from the key.
    body[:organizationId] = @organization_id

    request = Net::HTTP::Post.new(BASE.path + path)
    request["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
    request["x-api-key"] = @api_key
    request.body = JSON.generate(body)

    response = Net::HTTP.start(
      BASE.host, BASE.port,
      use_ssl: true,
      open_timeout: 5,
      read_timeout: 5,
    ) { |http| http.request(request) }

    raise "PULSE #{path}: #{response.code}" unless response.is_a?(Net::HTTPSuccess)

    JSON.parse(response.body)
  end
end

Four PULSE products that work on your product data, not your traffic. Find the missing facts that cost buying decisions, fix them in the right order, prove the fix, and keep it fixed.

Most of what stops a shopper buying is a fact your catalogue does not record: the screen size, the
fit, whether it works with what they already own. These four products find those gaps and prove
the repairs, from a catalogue export and your order history. No storefront change, no tracking
script, no traffic needed.

Product The question it answers Call Counts toward usage 
--- --- --- --- 
Decision Audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-audit) Which missing facts cost the most buying decisions, and which do I fix first? POST /catalog/audit Yes 
Decision Verification (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-verification) Did the repair actually make the catalogue answer what shoppers ask? POST /catalog/verify with repairs Yes 
Decision Monitor (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-monitor) What has slipped since the last export, and where? POST /catalog/verify without repairs Yes 
Return Verification (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/return-verification) Which missing facts go with returns, and did a repair move them? POST /outcomes No 
Promotion Audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/promotion-audit) Which vouchers, price cuts and free shipping paid for themselves after returns, and where should I give nothing? POST /interventions/audit Yes

and whether the repairs moved them.

the catalogue you just repaired.

The PULSE Decision Audit ranks the missing product facts in your catalogue by how many buying decisions they cost, so your team fixes the right column first. One API call, one CSV.

A completeness score tells you which column is emptiest. The Decision Audit tells you which
missing fact is costing you sales, and those are rarely the same column. On our own 216-laptop
test shelf, processor was missing twice as often as screen size, yet screen size came up in 13 of
32 buying requirements and processor in 2. Fill the emptiest column first and you do the most visible work for the
least return.

Who it is for: the catalogue or e-commerce lead who has to decide where the content budget
goes this quarter, and the developer who wires the export in.

- Every attribute in priority order, ranked by decision information: how much closer a shopper
gets to a decision once the fact is recorded. What that means (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/concepts/what-the-audit-measures).
- Where each missing value already lives: in your own titles and descriptions (a parse, often
same-day), in a supplier feed (a mapping), or nowhere (someone has to find it).
- With amortisationHorizon, an action per attribute: record it once, or ask the shopper.
- Plain flags where the ranking may be wrong, rather than a confident number.

One category export as a CSV string, up to 2 MB, roughly 20,000 products. Nothing is stored
unless you ask. Every field: POST /catalog/audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/audit#post-catalogaudit).

Counts toward usage: yes, one request per audit.

Catalogues decay. A supplier changes a feed, a new range arrives without its sizes, a bulk edit
blanks a column. Nobody notices until sales on that shelf drop. Decision Monitor compares each

and after.

PULSE Decision Verification re-measures your catalogue after a repair and grades every claimed fix against what actually changed. Proof without waiting for traffic.

Your team, an agency or an enrichment tool says the gaps are filled. Decision Verification checks.
Send the export from before and after the work, list what was claimed, and get back what actually
changed, attribute by attribute, and which buying requirements the catalogue can now answer.

It needs no traffic and no A/B test. The proof is in the data, so it is ready the moment the
new export is.

Who it is for: whoever signs off the repair work, and anyone paying for enrichment who wants
to see it delivered.

- Per attribute, the share of products a shopper could decide on before and after: what
improved, what regressed, what did not move.
- Per claimed repair, how many products it actually gained, and how strong the evidence is.
- unverifiedClaims: anything claimed that the new export does not bear out.
- Buying requirements the catalogue can now answer, and any it newly cannot.
- With hours on each claim, the effort behind the result, and a one-line headline to report.

Add organizationId to keep the result; leave it out and the response says nothing was stored.
Every field: POST /catalog/verify (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/audit#post-catalogverify).

Counts toward usage: yes, one request per verification.

chunks.t:
PULSE Promotion Audit judges your vouchers, price cuts and free-shipping offers on the orders that stayed bought, after returns and failed deliveries, against doing nothing.

A voucher that lifts orders is not yet a voucher that paid. Some of those orders come back, some
are refused at the door, and some shoppers would have bought at full price anyway. The Promotion
Audit reads your own history and answers four questions.

1. Which offers left you better off than doing nothing? Each offer's expected contribution per
shopper counts orders kept, returns a listing could have prevented, every other return, and
failed deliveries.
2. For which shoppers, and how many? Per group you can see: new or repeat buyers, a region,
cash on delivery. Including where the answer is to give nothing.
3. Does fixing the listing beat a discount? A repair is one more option, its one-off cost spread
over the shoppers it reaches.
4. What do shoppers really pay elsewhere? Your price against the same product after vouchers,
cashback, coins and shipping, beside the sticker gap.

Who it is for: a seller who runs promotions on one or more marketplaces and wants to know which
ones to keep, before spending more.

Every rate comes from your history or a test you ran. An offer with too little history is never
recommended; neither is one that wins only inside the noise. In both cases the answer is a test,
with the group and the offer named. Margin per kept order has no default: it is always yours.

Call What it answers 
--- --- 
POST /interventions/audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/interventions#post-interventionsaudit) Your history in, measured offers and a decision per group out 
POST /interventions/decide (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/interventions#post-interventionsdecide) The same decision from rates you already measured 
POST /interventions/landed (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/interventions#post-interventionslanded) The price a shopper actually pays on each marketplace

chunks.h: Settings, and where they come from
chunks.t:
Return cost and failed-delivery cost fall back to defaults we maintain when you do not send them,
and every response says which values were yours and which were ours, in configuration. Saved
per-account settings are on the way; until then, send your own numbers with each call.

It does not promise more profit or fewer returns: nothing has been measured on your history yet.
It does not target individual shoppers, and it does not set prices for you.

PULSE Return Verification shows which missing product facts go with your returns, whether a repair moved them, and what that was worth at your own costs. Report order outcomes with one free API call.

A return rate tells you that something went wrong. The return reason tells you what: too large,
not as described, does not work with my device. Return Verification reads those reasons against
your catalogue and answers three questions.

1. Which missing product facts go with returns? For each attribute, the return rate where it is
missing against where it is recorded, within the same brand and price band.
2. Did a repair move them? After your team fills a gap, the repaired products are compared with
similar ones that were not repaired, over the same weeks.
3. What was that worth? A verified reduction, valued with the costs you give us, minus any
orders the repair may have cost.

Who it is for: merchants whose returns cost real money, which on cash-on-delivery marketplaces

Marketplace reason codes are often vague. A code like "return in original or sealed condition"
mixes a change of mind with a size problem. Where you can send the buyer's comment or the
marketplace's own reassessed reason, they are used, and the report shows how much of your return
volume the codes leave unclear.

There are two ways, and you can use both.

A one-off analysis Ongoing

- It is off until there is return history, and ranking is unchanged without it.

Why the emptiest column is usually the wrong one to fix, what a bit of decision information buys, and the three cases where the ranking is wrong.

The audit returns attributes in priority order. The order is the product, and it is not the order
you would get by counting blanks.

chunks.h: Why not just fix the emptiest column?
chunks.t:
Because emptiness and usefulness are different quantities, and on a real shelf they invert.

Here are two attributes from the 216-product laptop catalogue we use for our own research:

Attribute Missing on Rank by emptiness Rank by decision value 
--- --- --- --- 
Processor 162 of 216 1st last 
Screen size 80 of 216 4th 1st 

Processor is missing twice as often and almost nobody is deciding on it: it appears in 2 of the 32
buying requirements we tested. Screen size appears in 13. Fill processor everywhere and you have
done the most visible work on the dashboard and moved the fewest decisions.

This is the whole argument. 
A completeness score measures your catalogue against itself. The audit measures it against what
shoppers are trying to decide. Those produce different work orders, and only one of them is
ranked by what it buys.

chunks.h: What is a bit of decision information?
chunks.t:
One bit is one halving of the shelf.

If a shopper faces 216 products and an attribute splits them cleanly in two, that attribute is
worth one bit: it takes 216 to 108. Two bits takes it to 54. The audit reports what each attribute
would be worth if it were recorded everywhere, minus what it is worth today, and the
difference is what the repair buys.

This is why the number is not a percentage. A percentage tells you how full a column is. Bits tell
you how much closer a shopper gets to a decision when you fill it.

chunks.h: Where does the missing value already live?
chunks.t:
Often in text you already own. Before recommending that anyone type anything, the audit tries to
recover the value from your own titles and descriptions.

On that same laptop shelf, 161 of 216 missing screen sizes were already sitting in the product
titles. That is a parse, not a procurement project, and it changes what the repair costs enough
to change whether it is worth doing.

The audit reports each attribute's provenance so you can tell the two apart:

Where the fact is What the repair actually is 
--- --- 
Already in your text Extraction. Cheap, and often same-day 
In a supplier feed Mapping. A ticket, not a project 
Nowhere Acquisition. Someone has to go and find it

Three cases, and we would rather you heard them from us.

The recorded values are not representative. Simulating a complete catalogue can only draw on values your shelf already holds. If an attribute
is recorded on twenty products and those twenty are not typical of the range, the simulation is
wrong in a way we can name and cannot yet correct.

The requirements are not yours. The buying requirements we test against are typed from public category guides and filter rails. If
your shoppers want something those do not cover, the ranking will not know. Sending us your own
search and filter logs is what fixes this, and it is the single highest-value thing you can add.

The fact exists only in a photograph. A dietary claim printed on a pack, a material visible in an image. We can tell you the attribute
is missing from your fields. We cannot yet read it out of your imagery, and we will say so on the
row rather than quietly scoring it as absent.

What to check before you ship PULSE, what to watch in the first week, and the claims we will not make for you.

You have run an audit, repaired something, and possibly wired up the runtime. This page is the
end of the path: what to check before it goes in front of shoppers, and what to expect
afterwards.

chunks.h: What should I check before shipping?
chunks.t:
Keys are the right kind. A publishable key (pk_live_...) is designed to be visible in page source. A secret key is not,
and belongs only in a server guide. If a secret key reached a theme file or a client bundle,
revoke it now rather than after the deploy.

A held-back group exists. Decide what fraction of traffic never sees PULSE ranking, and keep it. Without a control arm you
cannot tell a good quarter from a good ranker, and you will not be able to answer the first
question your finance team asks.

Your own order is the fallback. If the engine is slow or unavailable, the page should render your existing order rather than an
empty shelf. Check it by pointing endpoint at a port nothing is listening on and loading the
page.

`init()` failure is visible to you. init() sends the automatic signals exactly once and swallows its own error. A session whose
init() failed stays thin for its whole life, and nothing in the page tells you. Log the
failure, or call
captureAutoSignals() (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/sdk#beyond-the-client) again on a later page load.

chunks.t:
Exposure is recorded. If you rank, call exposure() with what was actually rendered. A ranking you cannot tie to what
the shopper saw cannot be evaluated later, and the buffered call costs almost nothing.

and belongs only in a server guide. If a secret key reached a theme file or a client bundle,

chunks.h: What should I watch in the first week?
chunks.t:
Watch Why it matters 
--- --- 
Sessions with zero signals Almost always init() failing silently, or a key scoped to the wrong origin 
Abstention rate The engine declining to rank is working as designed. A sudden move in it usually means the catalogue changed, not the engine 
Audit readiness, re-run Catalogues decay. New products arrive unrecorded, and a shelf that scored well last quarter quietly stops 
Fallback rate How often your own order was served instead. Should be near zero and is not always

chunks.h: What will you not claim for me?
chunks.t:
Worth reading before you repeat anything from this site internally.

No uplift number. 
We have run no live revenue experiment. We will not quote a conversion lift, a return-rate
reduction or an ROI multiple, and any figure you see elsewhere attached to those words did not
come from us.

What we can show is a property of your catalogue: which requirements it can and cannot resolve,
before and after a repair. That is measured, it is reproducible, and it is not the same thing as
a sale.

Three more limits, stated plainly:

- A fact that exists only inside a photograph is one we can tell you is missing and cannot yet
recover for you. Extracting attributes from product imagery is research we are doing, not a
feature we ship.
- Our simulation of a complete catalogue can only use values your shelf already records. 
Where an attribute's recorded values do not represent its true range, the simulation is wrong
in a way we can name and cannot yet correct.
- We have no customers to name. When that changes we will say so with their permission.

Connect PULSE to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client, so an agent searches the documentation instead of guessing, and asks the Decision API which products really meet a shopper's requirements.

Every page on this site is available to an agent over the Model Context Protocol. An assistant
with this connected searches the documentation and quotes it, instead of recalling an endpoint
that may not exist.

Or point your client at it directly, with no install:

The same block works in Claude Code (.mcp.json), Cursor and anything else that speaks MCP over
stdio.

It runs on your machine, not ours. 
This site is a static export, so there is no server here to host an HTTP endpoint on. The
package runs wherever your agent runs and fetches the published documentation index, which
means nothing about your prompts or your code reaches us. The one exception is
resolve_products, which sends its own input to the PULSE API, and only once you set a key.

Tool What it does 
--- --- 
search_docs Full-text search across every page. Returns the matching section, its URL and a score 
get_page One page as Markdown, by path, such as /quickstart or /api/v1/audit 
list_pages Every page with its title, for orienting before a search 
resolve_products Which candidates meet the shopper's requirements, which fail, and which the listing cannot tell, with what is missing. Needs an API key 

The three docs tools take a lang of en or vi.

chunks.h: How does an agent decide with it?
chunks.t:
An agent asked to recommend a product has two bad options without it: recommend from what it
thinks it read, or refuse. resolve_products gives it a third: say exactly what the listings
show. It calls POST /decide (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/decide), so add your key to the config:

Ask "which of these laptops have at least 16GB of RAM and cost under $1,500?" and the agent
gets, per laptop, fits, fails or cannot_tell, with the missing facts named. A product
whose listing never states its RAM is reported as exactly that, rather than guessed into the
answer or silently dropped. Each call counts as one decision on your plan.

chunks.h: Why is the search lexical rather than semantic?
chunks.t:
The website embeds your question with a model it has already downloaded. Making an agent download
one to ask a question is a poor trade, because the agent is itself a language model: it can read
three candidate sections and decide which is right far better than a cosine can.

It also matters that an agent asking about /catalog/audit wants the page containing that exact
string, and lexical scoring is precise about that where an embedding blurs it.

chunks.h: What if I want it pointed somewhere else?
chunks.t:
Set PULSE_DOCS_ORIGIN to serve from a different origin, which is mostly useful when you are
working on the documentation itself:

c.s: PULSE_DOCS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:3000 npx @thepulseapi/docs-mcp

chunks.h: Can I just read the Markdown?
chunks.t:
Yes, and you do not need MCP for it.

--- --- 
/llms.txt (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/llms.txt) Every page, titled and linked, in one file 
/llms-full.txt (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/llms-full.txt) The whole documentation as one Markdown document 
/llms.mdx/docs/<path /content.md Any single page as Markdown 
/search-index.json (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/search-index.json) The chunked corpus with its embeddings 

Each page also carries a Copy Markdown button, which is the fastest route when you just want
to paste one page into a conversation.

What works on a hosted storefront today, and what is still a script tag rather than an app.

There is no PULSE app or plugin yet. 
Not in the Shopify App Store, not on the WordPress plugin directory, not in the Magento
Marketplace. Anyone telling you otherwise is describing a plan. What exists today is the
script tag, and it works on all three.

That is less of a limitation than it sounds. PULSE needs three things from a storefront: the
script, an init call with your keys, and signals describing what the shopper is looking at.
Every platform here can supply all three from its own theme templates, which is also the only
place that knows what page the shopper is on.

Worth being precise about what you give up by pasting a script instead:

Script tag, today An app or plugin 
--- --- --- 
Install Paste into a theme file One click, no theme edit 
Keys Typed into the theme Entered in an admin screen 
Survives a theme change No Yes 
Catalogue sync You send products per request Pushed and kept current 
Signals You write them per template Mapped for you 

The first four rows are convenience. The fifth is where the difference actually lives, and it is
also why a plugin is not just packaging: a good one knows what a "collection page" means on that
platform and sends the right signal without being told.

Anything that lets you add a script to a page can run the browser SDK, and anything that can
make an HTTPS request can call the API directly. If your platform is not listed, the
Alpine guide (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/frameworks/alpine) is the closest shape: a script tag and HTML attributes, no
build step. For server-side work, see Backend (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/backend).

Layout XML and a template block, which is how Magento adds a script.

Not on the Marketplace. 
No PULSE extension exists. This is a small module you add yourself, in the shape Magento
expects.

Magento does not take a pasted script tag. Markup belongs to a template, templates are attached
by layout XML, and both live in a module. That is three files before anything runs, which is the
platform rather than PULSE.

default.xml applies to every page, which is what you want for init.

src_type="url" is load bearing. Without it Magento treats the path as a local static asset and
tries to resolve it inside pub/static, where it does not exist.

c.s:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<page xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
      layout="1column"
      xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="urn:magento:framework:View/Layout/etc/page_configuration.xsd">
    <head>
        <script src="https://cdn.thepulseapi.com/sdk/v0/pulse.iife.js" src_type="url" async="true"/>
    </head>
    <body>
        <referenceContainer name="before.body.end">
            <block class="Magento\Framework\View\Element\Template"
                   name="pulse.init"
                   template="Pulse_Tracking::init.phtml"/>
        </referenceContainer>
    </body>
</page>

chunks.t:
Category and product pages each get their own layout handle, so each can attach its own block
without any conditional logic.

The equivalent file for products is catalog_product_view.xml. Each template sends one track
call built from the registry object its block resolves.

Keys belong in system configuration. 
Hard-coding them in a template means a deployment to change a key. A system.xml field read
through ScopeConfigInterface puts them in the admin, which is also where a store operator
expects to find them.

    <body>
        <referenceContainer name="before.body.end">
            <block class="Pulse\Tracking\Block\Category"
                   name="pulse.category"
                   template="Pulse_Tracking::category.phtml"/>
        </referenceContainer>
    </body>
</page>

Not an App Store app. 
This is a theme edit. It does not survive switching themes, and it puts your keys in a theme

Online Store → Themes → Edit code → layout/theme.liquid, just before </head:

Use the json filter, not quotes. 
{{ product.vendor json }} escapes the value properly. Wrapping it in your own quotes breaks
on the first vendor with an apostrophe in the name, and does it only for that vendor, which is
the kind of bug that reaches production.

<script>

    Pulse.track([
      { type: 'category_view', value: {{ collection.handle | json }} }
    ]);
  });
</script>

Shopify fires its own events. Forward the ones that mean something.

The event name varies by theme: Dawn and its descendants publish cart:item-added, older themes
publish their own. Check what your theme dispatches before trusting this one.

<script>
  document.addEventListener('cart:item-added', function (event) {
    Pulse.event('add_to_cart', { productId: event.detail?.id });
  });
</script>

Checkout. Shopify does not let a theme script run on checkout pages outside Plus, so purchase

wp_enqueue_script in a small plugin, with signals from the WooCommerce conditionals.

Not on the plugin directory. 
There is no PULSE plugin to install. What follows is a short one you write yourself, which is
perhaps twenty lines and does not need to be anything more.

chunks.h: Write it as a plugin, not a theme edit
chunks.t:
Put it in wp-content/plugins/pulse-tracking/pulse-tracking.php. A theme edit disappears the
next time the theme updates; a plugin does not, and a child theme is more work than this.

Keys go in wp-config.php, not in the plugin file:

c.s:
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: PULSE tracking
 * Description: Loads the PULSE SDK and sends signals from WooCommerce templates.
 * Version: 1.0.0
 */

defined('ABSPATH') || exit;

add_action('wp_enqueue_scripts', function () {
    wp_enqueue_script(
        'pulse-sdk',
        'https://cdn.thepulseapi.com/sdk/v0/pulse.iife.js',
        [],
        null,   // the CDN path is already versioned; a ?ver= query would only break caching
        true    // in the footer, so it never blocks the first paint
    );

    // wp_add_inline_script with 'after' guarantees this runs once the SDK has loaded,
    // which is what makes the global `Pulse` safe to touch here.
    wp_add_inline_script('pulse-sdk', sprintf(
        'Pulse.init({ apiKey: %s, organizationId: %s });',
        wp_json_encode(PULSE_API_KEY),
        wp_json_encode(PULSE_ORG_ID)
    ), 'after');

    $signals = pulse_signals_for_current_page();
    if ($signals) {
        wp_add_inline_script('pulse-sdk', 'Pulse.track(' . wp_json_encode($signals) . ');', 'after');
    }
});

chunks.t:
WooCommerce already answers "what is this page" through its conditional tags. The whole mapping
is one function.

wp_json_encode, every time. 
It is WordPress's json_encode with the flags already set for embedding in HTML. Building the
JavaScript by string concatenation breaks on the first product category with a quote in its
name, and only for that category.

For a purchase, woocommerce_thankyou runs on the order received page and has the order, which
is the right place to record revenue. Orders that complete off-site need the
server-side call (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/backend/php) instead.
From nothing to a ranked catalogue in about ten lines.

You need a PULSE merchant account with an active subscription; the
introduction (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/#get-your-account-ready) covers both. Then sign in to the
dashboard and open Integration → API keys.
Create a key, name it for where it will run, and copy it immediately.

Shown once. 
The full key is returned only at creation. Only its hash is stored. If you lose it, revoke it
and create another.

Your organization id is on the same page. You need both.

init() also captures device, referrer and time of day once per session, unless you pass
autoTrack: false.

Every result carries the signals that matched it, so you can show a shopper why, or show
yourself why when it looks wrong.

c.s:
const { results } = await pulse.search(products);

results[0].scoreBreakdown; // why this one came first

chunks.t: Every method on PulseClient, the config it takes, and the functions the package exports beside it.

Method Returns 
--- --- --- 
init(config) TrackResponse \ null Start a session and send the automatic signals once 
getSession() SessionResponse Current session and inferred personas 
getSessionId() string The current session id 
resetSession() void Clear it and start fresh 
onPersona(cb) void Subscribe to persona updates

Method Returns 
--- --- --- 
track(signals) TrackResponse Send shopper signals 
search(products, options?) SearchResponse Rank products you pass in 
rankedCatalog(options?) RankedCatalogResponse Rank the catalogue already synced to PULSE 
event(type, data?) EventResponse Record a named event 

search and rankedCatalog are not interchangeable. search ranks what you hand it;
rankedCatalog ranks what PULSE already holds.

Method 
--- --- --- 
exposure(decisionId, items) void Record what was actually rendered, buffered 
flushExposures() Promise<void Send buffered exposures now

PulseClient is most of the package and not all of it. These are exported too, for the cases
where you need a signal without a client, or need to look at what the SDK cached.

init() calls captureAutoSignals() for you when autoTrack is on, so you only need these
directly when you want a signal at a different moment, or want one the automatic set leaves out.

Export Returns 
--- --- --- 
captureAutoSignals() Signal[] Device, referrer and time in one call. What init() sends 
captureDeviceSignal() Signal \ null Device class from the user agent 
captureReferrerSignal() Signal \ null Where the visit came from 
captureTimeSignal() Signal Time of day. Never null, there is always a clock 
captureEnhancedReferrerSignals() Signal[] Campaign and channel detail beyond the plain referrer 
captureDeviceInfoAsync(): Promise DeviceInfo Fuller device detail, including client hints 
captureGeoInfo(): Promise GeoInfo \ null Coarse location from the IP 
geoToSignals(geo) Signal[] Turn a GeoInfo into signals 
captureWeatherInfo(lat, lon, apiKey?): Promise WeatherInfo \ null Conditions at a point 
weatherToSignals(weather) Signal[] Turn a WeatherInfo into signals 
captureCulturalCalendar(countryCode) Signal[] Seasonal and cultural events active today 
parseUserAgent(ua) DeviceInfo Parse a user agent string you already have

captureWeatherInfo needs your own key. 
It calls OpenWeatherMap and returns null without an apiKey, so nothing breaks if you leave
it out. The free tier is 1,000 calls a day, which is why the result is cached per session
rather than fetched per page.

captureAutoSignals() is exported for one specific failure. init() sends the automatic
signals exactly once and swallows its own error, so a session whose init() failed never
re-sends them and stays thin for its whole life. These signals cost no network of their own, so
calling this again on a later page load is cheaper than the alternative.

Device, location and weather are properties of the session rather than of the page: they cannot
change between one page and the next. The SDK captures them once, keys the cache by session id so
it cannot outlive the visitor it describes, and reuses it. You rarely need to touch this.

Export Returns 
--- --- --- 
readSessionContext(sessionId) SessionContext \ null The cache, or null if it belongs to another session 
writeSessionContext(sessionId, patch) void Merge fields into it 
isWeatherFresh(ctx, now?) boolean Whether the weather reading is still inside its TTL 
clearSessionContext() void Drop the cache 
WEATHER_TTL_MS number 10 minutes 

Weather is the only field here with a TTL. Everything else is immutable for the session, but a
30-minute session can outlast a rain shower, and a weather:rain signal driving a
recommendation after the sun came out is the engine being confidently wrong.

PULSE storefront products rank your catalogue for each live visit, anonymously. Decision API, Search, Recommendations and category pages, each with the reason behind every score.

A thousand shoppers land on the same page and see the same grid, though they came for different
things. The storefront products read what the current visit implies, from the pages viewed, the
filters set and the words searched, and order your products for it. No login, no cookies, no
personal data, and every score comes with the factors that produced it.

Product What it ranks Calls Counts toward usage 
--- --- --- --- 
Decision API (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/storefront/decision-api) The live session itself: what this visit is shopping for POST /track, POST /session Yes 
Search (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/storefront/search) Search results, from your engine or ours POST /search, POST /rerank, POST /suggest Yes, /suggest free 
Recommendations (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/storefront/recommendations) A recommendation strip, on a first visit too POST /catalog/ranked with recommendCount Yes 
Category pages (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/storefront/category-pages) Category and landing-page grids POST /catalog/ranked with categorySlug Yes 

Measuring is free: POST /event and POST /exposure record what was shown and what happened, so
you can prove the ranking worked, and they never count toward usage.

chunks.h: Built to run beside what you have
chunks.t:
- It falls back to your own order. If PULSE is slow or unreachable, the shopper sees the order
you would have shown anyway.
- A share of visits is always held back, ranked without PULSE, so the difference can be
measured rather than asserted.
- It reads Southeast Asian searches in Vietnamese, Thai, Bahasa and English, prices included.

Get the catalogue right first: ranking can only surface facts your catalogue records. The
catalogue products (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue) find and fix the gaps.

PULSE orders category and landing-page grids for whoever arrived, so a campaign that sends a thousand people to one page shows each of them the products they came for.

A campaign sends a thousand people to one category page, and all of them see the same grid. The
shopper who came from a price-comparison link and the one who came from a gift guide want
different products first. PULSE orders the grid against what each visit implies, with a held-back
share of visits shown your default order, so the difference can be measured.

Who it is for: merchandisers running campaigns and landing pages, and any category with more
products than fit above the fold.

- categorySlug takes your own slug or a parent one; leave it out to rank the whole catalogue.
- The whole category is ranked and limit, up to 200, only decides how much comes back, so page
two continues the same order.
- Pass signals on the same call to record what the visitor just did before ranking.

With the SDK: await pulse.rankedCatalog({ limit: 24 }). Reference:
POST /catalog/ranked (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/ranking#post-catalogranked).

Counts toward usage: yes, one request per page.

c.s:
curl -X POST "https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/catalog/ranked" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: pk_live_..." \
  -d '{
    "sessionId": "sess_abc123",
    "organizationId": "org_abc123",
    "categorySlug": "helmets-safety",
    "page": 1,
    "limit": 24
  }'

chunks.t:
The PULSE Decision API reads an anonymous visit as it happens and says what the shopper is shopping for, so every ranking call that follows is personal from the first click.

Personalisation usually starts after a login or weeks of history. The Decision API starts at the
first page view. Each signal you send, a category opened, a price filter set, a query typed, sharpens
its read of what this visit is shopping for, and every ranking call afterwards uses it.

Who it is for: storefronts with anonymous traffic, which is most of it, and teams that will not
store personal data to personalise.

- The personas inferred so far for the session, each scored from 0 to 1, from POST /session
or as the response to each POST /track.
- Device, referrer and time read from the request itself, so even a call with no signals opens the
session with something to go on.
- A session that decays as the visit moves on, so an old interest does not outrank a new one.

From the browser, the SDK does the same in one line: await pulse.track([...]). Full reference:
POST /track (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/track) and POST /session (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/session). The signal types are in
Signals (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/concepts/signals).

Counts toward usage: yes, per /track and /session call.

PULSE Recommendations rank a strip against the visit happening now, so a first-time shopper gets relevant picks without any purchase history. One call, alongside the page it sits on.

Most recommendation engines need history: past purchases, a login, weeks of clicks. A first-time
visitor gets the bestsellers, which is everyone's strip. PULSE ranks the strip against what this
visit implies, so the first session is served as well as the hundredth.

Who it is for: storefronts where most visitors are new or anonymous, which in Southeast Asian
marketplaces is most of them.

Ask for a strip on the same call that ranks the page. recommendCount returns that many products,
each ranked out of what is left after the page itself.

The response carries items for the page and recommendations for the strip, up to 50, each with
its score and, with includeBreakdown, the reason behind it. It ranks the catalogue you have
synced to PULSE. Reference: POST /catalog/ranked (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/ranking#post-catalogranked).

Counts toward usage: yes, one request for the page and its strip together.

c.s:
curl -X POST "https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/catalog/ranked" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: pk_live_..." \
  -d '{
    "sessionId": "sess_abc123",
    "organizationId": "org_abc123",
    "categorySlug": "headphones",
    "recommendCount": 6,
    "includeBreakdown": true
  }'

chunks.t:
PULSE Search ranks results on what the shopper is deciding, not only on matching words. Keep your search engine and rerank its results, or let PULSE rank the products you pass in. Reads Vietnamese, Thai, Bahasa and English.

Two shoppers type "headphones". One is buying a gift under a budget, the other wants noise
cancelling for travel. Word matching shows them the same list. PULSE Search ranks each list for the
visit it belongs to, and reads the rest of the query too: a price limit, who it is for, the
occasion, whether it is urgent.

Who it is for: any storefront with a search box, whether you keep your current engine or not.

You have Call What it does 
--- --- --- 
A search engine you are keeping POST /rerank Reorders the results it already returned. The lightest way in 
Products in hand, no engine POST /search Ranks the products you pass, against the session 
A search box POST /suggest Query suggestions scored on the session. Free, since it fires on every keystroke

c.s:
const { results } = await pulse.search(products, { query: "tai nghe cho mẹ dưới 1tr5", limit: 24 });

results[0].scoreBreakdown; // why this product came first, factor by factor

Every result carries its score breakdown: fit to the session, quality, text match, price, and,
when you send return history, how often it stays bought. What a score is made of (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/ranking#what-a-score-is-made-of).

Counts toward usage: yes for /search and /rerank; /suggest is free.

Chào mừng bạn đến với tài liệu dành cho nhà phát triển của PULSE, dành cho nhà bán hàng đã có tài khoản PULSE và gói đăng ký. Kết nối danh mục và cửa hàng, tìm ra thông tin sản phẩm còn thiếu đang làm mất doanh số, và chứng minh từng bản sửa có tác dụng.

Chào mừng bạn đến với tài liệu dành cho nhà phát triển của PULSE. Kết nối danh mục sản phẩm và cửa
hàng trực tuyến của bạn với PULSE, tìm ra thông tin sản phẩm còn thiếu đang làm bạn mất doanh số,
và chứng minh từng bản sửa có tác dụng. Làm theo các bước bên dưới để chuẩn bị tài khoản, hoặc
chuyển thẳng tới hướng dẫn nhanh (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/quickstart).

Dành cho nhà bán hàng dùng PULSE. 
Tài liệu này dành cho các nhà bán hàng trực tuyến đã có tài khoản nhà bán hàng PULSE và gói
đăng ký đang hoạt động, cùng các lập trình viên họ mời vào để kết nối. Mọi yêu cầu đều cần một
khóa API, và khóa đó được tạo trong trang quản trị của tài khoản. Nếu công ty bạn chưa có tài
khoản, hãy xem các gói dịch vụ và tạo tài khoản.

PULSE là dịch vụ dành cho nhà bán hàng thương mại điện tử. PULSE đọc danh mục sản phẩm của bạn và đo
xem nó có trả lời được những câu người mua hỏi trước khi mua hay không: màn hình bao nhiêu inch, có
vừa không, có dùng được với thứ họ đang có không. Ở chỗ danh mục không trả lời được, PULSE cho bạn
biết thông tin còn thiếu nào làm mất nhiều quyết định mua nhất, nên sửa chỗ nào trước, và sau đó
bản sửa có tác dụng hay không.

PULSE được bán thành từng sản phẩm, mỗi sản phẩm là một API và dùng được riêng:

- Decision Audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-audit). Gửi một ngành hàng; nhận lại các thuộc tính đáng ghi, xếp theo số người mua
cần đến chúng.
- Decision Verification (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-verification). Gửi danh mục đã sửa; nhận lại những gì đã thay đổi, theo từng thuộc
tính.
- Return Verification (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/return-verification). Gửi đơn hàng kèm lý do người mua đưa
ra; xem thông tin còn thiếu nào đi cùng hàng bị trả, và bản sửa có làm chúng giảm không.
- Decision Monitor (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/decision-monitor). Gửi mỗi bản xuất mới; xem nhóm hàng nào bị tụt
so với lần trước.
- Promotion Audit (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/catalogue/promotion-audit). Gửi lịch sử khuyến mãi; xem ưu đãi nào thực sự có
lãi sau khi trừ hàng bị trả và giao thất bại, và chỗ nào không nên ưu đãi.
- Sản phẩm cho cửa hàng (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/storefront), không bắt buộc: Decision API, Search, Recommendations và
trang danh mục xếp hạng danh mục cho từng khách truy cập dựa trên những gì phiên truy cập cho
thấy, kèm lý do cho mỗi điểm số.

PULSE do Resolve Labs làm ra. Trang giới thiệu, nói về lý do thay vì cách làm, là
thepulseapi.com.

Tạo tài khoản nhà bán hàng. Đăng ký tại thepulseapi.com bằng email công việc. Tổ chức của bạn được
xem xét trước khi kích hoạt, và bạn nhận được email khi được duyệt.

Chọn gói đăng ký. So sánh các gói trên trang bảng giá, rồi đăng ký tại
Settings → Billing trong trang quản trị. Gói của bạn quyết định số yêu cầu
mà các khóa được phép gửi mỗi tháng.

Tạo khóa API. Trong trang quản trị, mở Integration → API keys, tạo một khóa và sao chép
ngay: khóa chỉ hiển thị một lần. Mã tổ chức nằm trên cùng trang đó. Mọi ví dụ trên trang này đều cần
cả hai, và gửi tới.

chunks.h: Sản phẩm này thực sự giải quyết vấn đề gì?
chunks.t:
Một người mua rời đi mà không mua gì. Hoặc là họ không tìm thấy sản phẩm, hoặc là danh mục của bạn
không giúp họ phân biệt được các sản phẩm với nhau.

Vế thứ hai lớn hơn và gần như không ai đo nó. Trên một kệ thử nghiệm 216 sản phẩm chúng tôi dựng, gồm 156 mẫu laptop tạo sẵn và 60 sản phẩm thật từ một sàn thương mại điện tử,
94 sản phẩm vẫn không thể phân biệt được sau mọi câu hỏi mà người mua có thể trả lời, bởi vì
những thuộc tính giúp tách chúng ra không được ghi ở đâu cả. Không mô hình xếp hạng nào sửa được
điều đó. Chỉ có việc ghi lại thuộc tính mới sửa được.

Nên PULSE bắt đầu từ danh mục chứ không phải từ phiên truy cập:

Dữ kiện đó vốn đang nằm ở đâu? Thường là trong chính tiêu đề và mô tả của bạn, lấy lại được trước khi ai đó phải gõ gì 
Bản sửa có tác dụng không? Cùng một phép đo trên tệp xuất đã sửa, không cần lưu lượng truy cập

chunks.t:
Sáu bước, theo đúng thứ tự bạn sẽ gặp. Mỗi bước tự nó đã hữu ích, và bạn có thể dừng lại sau bất

chunks.t: Framework (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/frameworks) · Gian hàng (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/platforms) · Máy chủ (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/backend)

kèm danh sách sản phẩm bị ảnh hưởng. Không lưu trạng thái, và không lưu gì trừ khi bạn yêu cầu.

Chạy bản kiểm tra đầu tiên (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/quickstart)

Thứ hạng được đo bằng bit thông tin quyết định, không phải đoán từ lượt nhấp, và cột trống nhất
thường là cột không đáng sửa nhất.

Bản kiểm tra đo gì (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/concepts/what-the-audit-measures)

Đội của bạn điền thuộc tính đứng đầu bảng. POST /catalog/verify chạy lại đúng phép đo đó trên
tệp xuất đã sửa và báo cáo điều gì đã thay đổi, theo từng thuộc tính. Nó đọc danh mục chứ không
đọc lưu lượng, nên không phải chờ gì cả.

Tài liệu endpoint (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/api/v1/audit)

chunks.h: Đưa vào hệ thống của bạn
chunks.t:
Chỉ cần khi bạn muốn dùng phần thời gian thực. Có hướng dẫn cho React, Vue, Angular, Astro, Alpine
và Laravel; hướng dẫn gian hàng cho Shopify, WordPress và Magento; hướng dẫn máy chủ cho tám ngôn
ngữ.

Framework (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/frameworks) · Gian hàng (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/platforms) · Máy chủ (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/backend)

chunks.h: Xếp hạng phiên truy cập, nếu bạn muốn
chunks.t:
Phần tuỳ chọn, và là phần duy nhất chạm tới gian hàng của bạn. SDK gửi tín hiệu, bộ máy xếp hạng
danh mục theo những gì phiên truy cập hàm ý, và mọi điểm số đều kèm diễn giải theo từng yếu tố.

Tài liệu SDK (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/sdk) · Tài liệu API (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/api/v1)

Cần kiểm tra gì trước khi phát hành, cần theo dõi gì sau đó, và những điều chúng tôi sẽ không
tuyên bố.

Đưa lên production (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/going-live)

Hoặc nhúng thẳng vào trang, đây là cách các bản tích hợp gian hàng đang dùng:

Thẻ script này expose client ra biến toàn cục Pulse, nên gọi Pulse.init(...) là chạy được ngay.

Những gì rời khỏi trình duyệt. 
Tín hiệu và một mã phiên. Không có tên, không có email, không có dữ liệu thanh toán. Bản kiểm
tra thì không nhìn thấy người mua nào cả: nó đọc dữ liệu sản phẩm.

chunks.h: Cần biết gì trước khi tin vào các con số?

chunks.t:
Mọi thay đổi trên các trang này, mới nhất trước, đọc trực tiếp từ git khi dựng site chứ không viết tay.

Trang này ghi lại điều gì đã thay đổi trên site và vào lúc nào. Danh sách được đọc từ lịch sử của
chính kho mã khi site được dựng, nên nó không thể lệch khỏi những gì thực sự đã xảy ra và không ai
phải nhớ cập nhật nó.

Đây không phải nhật ký thay đổi của API. 
Quy tắc tương thích của API, thế nào là thay đổi phá vỡ, và chúng tôi có trách nhiệm gì khi điều
đó xảy ra, nằm ở Phiên bản (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/vi/api/versioning). API được đánh phiên bản theo URL còn các
hướng dẫn thì không, đó là lựa chọn có chủ đích và được giải thích ở trang đó. Trang này là
lịch sử của chính bộ tài liệu.
Nội dung commit được giữ nguyên tiếng Anh, vì đó là ngôn ngữ của kho mã.

chunks.h: Xem lịch sử của từng trang
chunks.t:
Mỗi trang đều hiển thị ngày sửa đổi gần nhất ở cuối trang, kèm liên kết tới toàn bộ lịch sử commit
của riêng tệp đó. Đây là cách nhanh nhất để trả lời câu hỏi "tháng trước trang này có viết khác
không", vốn thường mới là câu hỏi thật sự.

Các trang là tệp MDX trong
content/docs (https://github.com/mypulseapi/handbook/tree/main/content/docs), nên lịch sử chính
là git thông thường: mọi lần sửa, ai sửa, và những gì khác đã thay đổi trong cùng một commit.

Kết nối tài liệu PULSE với Claude, Cursor hoặc bất kỳ MCP client nào, để tác tử tìm và đọc đúng trang thay vì đoán.

Mọi trang trên site này đều có thể truy cập bằng tác tử qua Model Context Protocol. Một trợ lý đã
kết nối sẽ tìm trong tài liệu và trích dẫn, thay vì nhớ nhầm một endpoint không tồn tại.

Hoặc trỏ thẳng client của bạn vào đó, không cần cài:

Cùng khối cấu hình đó dùng được cho Claude Code (.mcp.json), Cursor và mọi thứ nói MCP qua stdio.

Nó chạy trên máy bạn, không phải máy chúng tôi. 
Site này là bản xuất tĩnh nên ở đây không có máy chủ nào để dựng một endpoint HTTP. Gói này chạy
ở nơi tác tử của bạn chạy và tải chỉ mục tài liệu đã xuất bản, nghĩa là không có gì về câu lệnh
hay mã nguồn của bạn đi tới chúng tôi. Ngoại lệ duy nhất là resolve_products, công cụ gửi chính
dữ liệu đầu vào của nó tới API PULSE, và chỉ khi bạn đã đặt khóa.

Công cụ Làm gì 
--- --- 
search_docs Tìm toàn văn trên mọi trang. Trả về đúng mục khớp, URL và điểm số 
get_page Một trang dạng Markdown, theo đường dẫn, ví dụ /quickstart hay /api/v1/audit 
list_pages Mọi trang kèm tiêu đề, để định hướng trước khi tìm 
resolve_products Sản phẩm nào đáp ứng yêu cầu của người mua, sản phẩm nào không, và sản phẩm nào trang sản phẩm không đủ thông tin để biết, kèm thông tin còn thiếu. Cần khóa API 

Ba công cụ tài liệu nhận lang là en hoặc vi.

chunks.h: Tác tử ra quyết định với nó như thế nào?
chunks.t:
resolve_products gọi POST /decide (https://developer.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/decide). Thêm khóa vào cấu hình bằng
"env": { "PULSE_API_KEY": "pk_live_..." }. Với mỗi sản phẩm, tác tử nhận fits, fails
hoặc cannot_tell, kèm tên thông tin còn thiếu, thay vì đoán. Mỗi lần gọi tính là một quyết định
trong gói của bạn.

chunks.h: Vì sao tìm theo từ khoá chứ không phải theo ngữ nghĩa?
chunks.t:
Website nhúng câu hỏi của bạn bằng một mô hình mà nó đã tải sẵn. Bắt một tác tử tải mô hình chỉ để
đặt câu hỏi là đánh đổi không đáng, vì bản thân tác tử đã là một mô hình ngôn ngữ: nó đọc ba mục
ứng viên và tự quyết định tốt hơn nhiều so với một phép cosine.

Thêm nữa, một tác tử hỏi về /catalog/audit muốn đúng trang chứa chuỗi đó, và tìm theo từ khoá
chính xác ở điểm này trong khi embedding thì làm nhoè đi.

chunks.h: Muốn trỏ sang nơi khác thì sao?
chunks.t:
Đặt PULSE_DOCS_ORIGIN để đọc từ một origin khác, chủ yếu hữu ích khi bạn đang sửa chính tài liệu
này:

c.s: PULSE_DOCS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:3000 npx @thepulseapi/docs-mcp
